items.prompt: Per L1, what's the difference between a claim about "capacity" and a claim about "capability"?
choices: Capacity is about not having room given current commitments; capability is about whether someone is able to do the work at all
They are two different words for the exact same underlying claim
Capacity refers only to physical office space, while capability refers to skill
Capability is always a stronger claim than capacity, so the two can be used interchangeably
items.explanation: L1 distinguishes these as genuinely different claims — one about available room given existing commitments, the other about ability — a bare 'no' doesn't distinguish them.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, is the engineer's actual concern about capacity or about capability?
choices: Capacity — they don't have room for a fourth project given three already-committed ones, not doubt about their ability to do the work
Capability — the engineer doubts they have the skills needed for the Meridian migration
Neither — the engineer has no real concern and is looking for an excuse
It's impossible to tell from the Scenario's facts which one is the actual concern
items.explanation: The Scenario is explicit that the constraint is workload capacity, not a skills or ability question.

items.prompt: What is "sustainable boundary-setting" as this unit defines it?
choices: The practice of surfacing capacity limits as they're reached, so workload decisions get made deliberately instead of by default through silent overextension
The practice of refusing all new work requests as a fixed policy
A formal HR process for filing workload complaints
The practice of only ever working the exact hours listed in an employment contract
items.explanation: Sustainable boundary-setting is specifically about deliberate, visible trade-off decisions — not blanket refusal, HR processes, or rigid hour-counting.

items.prompt: Per L1, is the goal of sustainable boundary-setting to avoid taking on any new work?
choices: No — the goal is making sure new work gets added with an explicit trade-off acknowledged, not avoiding new work altogether
Yes — the goal is described as minimizing total work accepted at all costs
No, but only because refusing new work is against most companies' policies
Yes, but only during promotion cycles specifically
items.explanation: L1 explicitly frames the goal as making trade-offs visible and deliberate, not as refusing new work as a blanket policy.

items.prompt: What is a "capacity signal"?
choices: A factual statement of current workload and commitments, offered as context rather than as an excuse or a refusal
A formal written notice submitted to HR about being overworked
A vague statement like "I'm pretty busy" with no specifics attached
A performance review metric tracked by a manager
items.explanation: A capacity signal is specifically a factual, contextual statement — not an HR filing, a vague complaint, or a formal metric.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, what would a genuine capacity signal from the engineer include?
choices: Naming the specific projects (Atlas rollout, billing fix, Q3 reporting) already committed to, with their real deadlines
A general statement that they've been feeling stressed lately
A comparison of their workload to a coworker's workload
A request for a raise tied to their current workload
items.explanation: A credible capacity signal names specific, concrete commitments — not general feelings, peer comparisons, or compensation requests.

items.prompt: What is "trade-off framing"?
choices: Presenting a new request alongside its real cost, rather than giving a flat yes or no
A negotiation tactic used exclusively in salary discussions
A framework for evaluating a company's overall business strategy
A method for splitting credit between team members on a shared project
items.explanation: Trade-off framing is specifically about surfacing the real cost of saying yes — not salary negotiation, business strategy, or credit-splitting.

items.prompt: Does trade-off framing mean the person raising the constraint decides unilaterally what happens next?
choices: No — it puts the actual decision in the requester's hands, since they usually have context about relative priority that the person raising the constraint doesn't
Yes — trade-off framing means making the final call and simply informing the requester afterward
No, because trade-off framing means automatically declining the new request every time
Yes, but only if the person raising the constraint has more seniority than the requester
items.explanation: L1/L2 describe trade-off framing as surfacing the trade-off and handing the decision to the requester, not deciding unilaterally.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, what specifically makes the engineer hesitant to just say "no" to the new request?
choices: Fear that declining will look like an inability to handle a full workload, especially with promotion season approaching
The engineer doesn't actually have any other active projects to point to
Company policy explicitly forbids ever declining a manager's request
The engineer has never spoken to this particular manager before
items.explanation: The Scenario explicitly names the promotion-season timing and the fear of looking incapable as the source of hesitation.

items.prompt: Per L1's closing question, what's the actual alternative being sought — beyond "yes, and burn out" or "no, and look incapable"?
choices: A way to decline or negotiate that makes the real capacity constraint visible without it reading as an admission of inability
A way to avoid ever having this kind of conversation with a manager again
A way to get the manager to stop assigning any further work permanently
A way to transfer the decision entirely to HR instead of handling it directly
items.explanation: L1 frames the sought alternative as a middle path — surfacing the real constraint — not permanent avoidance or escalation to HR.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does a bare "No, I can't" risk being heard as, absent other context?
choices: An unexplained capability judgment — reluctance or overwhelm — rather than an informed capacity statement
A neutral, universally-understood statement with no risk of misinterpretation
A formal legal declaration with binding consequences
An explicit compliment to the requester's judgment
items.explanation: L2's table specifically identifies the risk of a bare 'no' being heard as a capability judgment, since it gives the listener nothing else to work with.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does naming specific existing commitments change how a decline is received, compared to a bare no?
choices: It shifts the conversation from "can this person do it" to "given everything already committed, does this new thing take priority over something else"
It has no real effect — both versions are received identically by most listeners
It works only because naming specific projects is required by company policy
It works only when the listener already personally knows about those projects
items.explanation: L2 explicitly frames the shift as reframing the conversation around prioritization rather than personal capability.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, who does trade-off framing hand the final decision to?
choices: The requester, since they usually have context (like relative urgency) that the person raising the constraint doesn't
The person raising the constraint, who decides unilaterally what happens next
A neutral third party, such as HR, in every case
Nobody — the decision is left permanently unresolved
items.explanation: L2's diagram shows the requester making the final call once the trade-off and capacity signal are visible — not the constraint-raiser, HR, or nobody.

items.prompt: Per L2, is handing the decision back to the requester unfair to the person raising the capacity constraint?
choices: No — it's framed as fairer to both people, since the requester gets to use authority they actually have, and the constraint-raiser isn't left guessing or silently sacrificing something
Yes — L2 states this approach is unfair and recommends against it
No, but only in organizations with fewer than 50 employees
Yes, but only when the requester is more senior than the person raising the constraint
items.explanation: L2 explicitly argues this is fairer to both parties, not a concession that disadvantages the person raising the constraint.

items.prompt: Per L2, would "I'm pretty busy right now" work as well as naming three specific projects?
choices: No — a vague capacity claim is easy to dismiss because it gives the listener nothing concrete to weigh against the new request
Yes — vague and specific capacity claims are described as equally effective
No, but only because "busy" is considered an unprofessional word choice
Yes, but only if said in a serious tone of voice
items.explanation: L2 explicitly contrasts vague claims (easy to dismiss) with specific, named commitments (concrete enough to actually weigh).

items.prompt: What makes a trade-off "real and specific enough to actually reason about," per L2?
choices: Naming the actual commitments at stake — which projects, what's already on the line
Using formal, legalistic language regardless of the actual content
Mentioning a specific dollar amount tied to the request
Involving a third-party mediator in the initial conversation
items.explanation: L2 ties specificity to naming actual, concrete commitments — not formal language, dollar figures, or mediation.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's the risk of silently absorbing new work instead of surfacing the trade-off?
choices: It hides the real cost from the person who could have made an informed call, and leads to the option to speak up eventually running out
There's no real risk — silently absorbing work is described as the safest long-term choice
The only risk is a minor, temporary inconvenience with no lasting effect
This failure mode applies only to remote work arrangements
items.explanation: L2 explicitly warns that silent absorption hides the trade-off from the person who could act on it and compounds over time.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's wrong with deciding unilaterally which existing commitment should slip, without surfacing that to the requester?
choices: It removes the requester's ability to weigh in on a call that's often actually theirs to make
Nothing is wrong with this approach — L2 recommends it as the default
It's only a problem if the decision turns out to be the wrong one in hindsight
It's a problem only in organizations with a strict, formal chain of command
items.explanation: L2 frames unilateral trade-off decisions as removing the requester's legitimate say in a prioritization call that's often theirs to make.

items.prompt: In L3's worked hallway response, what two things does the engineer's answer actually do?
choices: Makes the real trade-off visible and hands the prioritization decision to the manager
Refuses the request outright and ends the conversation immediately
Agrees to take on Meridian with no conditions or trade-offs mentioned
Asks the manager to file a formal workload complaint with HR
items.explanation: L3 explicitly describes the response as surfacing the trade-off and handing the decision to the manager — not an outright refusal or unconditional yes.

items.prompt: Per L3, does the engineer's response name specific projects, or refer to workload only in general terms?
choices: It names three specific projects (Atlas rollout, billing fix, Q3 reporting) with real deadlines
It refers only to being "really busy lately" with no specifics
It refers to workload only by citing a percentage of total capacity used
It doesn't mention workload at all, only the engineer's personal feelings
items.explanation: L3's worked example specifically names concrete projects, consistent with L2's point about credible, specific capacity signals.

items.prompt: Per L3, why doesn't naming three other projects just amount to a longer way of saying no?
choices: It gives the listener a specific, checkable reason and an actual offer, which reads as someone actively managing a real workload rather than avoiding work
It doesn't actually differ from a bare no in any meaningful way
It differs only because it takes longer to say, which alone changes the perception
It differs only if the listener already personally trusts the speaker
items.explanation: L3 explains the difference in terms of what the listener is left to conclude — a specific, checkable reason plus an offer, versus an unexplained refusal.

items.prompt: Per L3, what are most managers actually looking for regarding a report's capacity, according to this unit?
choices: People who make workload trade-offs visible, rather than infinite capacity or silent overloading
Employees who never decline any request under any circumstances
Employees who handle every request without ever mentioning existing commitments
People who file a written capacity report every single week
items.explanation: L3 explicitly states managers generally aren't seeking infinite capacity — they want trade-offs surfaced rather than silent overload.

items.prompt: When the manager pushes back ("can you just find a way to fit it in?"), what does L3 say this pushback usually actually means?
choices: The manager usually needs more specific information to make the prioritization call, not that the original trade-off was wrong
The manager is always testing the engineer's commitment to the company
The pushback means the engineer's original framing was a mistake and should be retracted entirely
The pushback is always a sign the engineer should escalate immediately to HR
items.explanation: L3 explicitly reframes pushback as a request for more specific decision-making information, not proof the original approach was wrong.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does the engineer repeat a specific trade-off rather than giving in to the pushback?
choices: Giving in would let the "urgent" framing override the actual capacity constraint without anyone consciously deciding that was the right call
Repeating the trade-off is purely a stalling tactic with no real purpose
Giving in is actually the recommended response, and the engineer's persistence is presented as a mistake
The engineer repeats it only because company policy requires a minimum of two exchanges before agreeing to anything
items.explanation: L3 frames holding the trade-off as keeping the decision honest and deliberate, rather than letting urgency framing silently override the real constraint.

items.prompt: Per L3's "what generalizes" section, does this unit's lesson apply only to workplace project assignments?
choices: No — it generalizes to any situation with competing, legitimate demands on limited time, including volunteer commitments and family obligations
Yes — the lesson is stated to apply exclusively to engineering project assignments
No, but only to situations involving a direct manager specifically
Yes, but only during promotion cycles specifically
items.explanation: L3 explicitly extends the core lesson beyond workplace project assignments to any competing-demands situation.

items.prompt: Per L3, should the exact three projects and specific trade-off from this worked example be reused as-is for a different person's boundary-setting conversation?
choices: No — a different person's real trade-offs will involve different projects, different stakes, and possibly a different answer about what should move
Yes — the same three projects and trade-off apply universally to any workplace boundary-setting conversation
Yes, but only for other engineers at the same company
No — L3 states this exact example should never be referenced again under any circumstances
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that the specific projects and trade-off are this engineer's actual situation — the transferable part is the method, not this exact content.
